item.text: {"batch_notes":["Batch-wide calibration is constrained because only one dossier is available; no distinct adjacent ruler-period comparator exists in the manifest.","The dossier supports a mixed judgment: documented social-program implementation and coverage coexist with weak direct personal attribution, incomplete service-quality evidence, and a ruler-attributed abrupt COVID-policy exit with potentially avoidable suffering.","Official statistics and policy records are treated as evidence of state implementation, not automatically as personal Xi attribution."],"calibration_batch_id":"chapter-judge:2023-population-top20-gate1-judges-v2:2023:6B","chapter_id":"6B","evaluations":[{"calibrated_against":[],"calibration_batch_id":"chapter-judge:2023-population-top20-gate1-judges-v2:2023:6B","chapter_id":"6B","chapter_rationale":"Xi Jinping's 2023 period shows genuine state-level welfare implementation: medical-insurance financing included a substantial government subsidy and a targeted rural low-income coverage objective (E024), major-disease insurance reached 11.56 million residents and basic insurance covered nearly one billion people (E025), education and social expenditure increased with rural-school and student-loan measures (E026), and rural household income grew faster than urban income (E027). These gains are meaningful but mostly indirectly attributed to Xi, with limited evidence on realized service quality, equal access, professional administration, transparent correction, political conditionality, and durable institutional effects. The strongest ruler-attributed discriminating evidence is the abrupt and reportedly chaotic zero-COVID exit and exclusion of certain foreign medical products from national insurance (E028), which weighs against a higher score because crisis management may have increased avoidable suffering. Overall, the contribution is mixed rather than clearly baseline-adjusted high performance.","chapter_specific":[{"field":"evidenced_service_domains","value":"Medical-insurance financing and coverage, major-disease insurance, education spending and rural-school support, student-loan relief, social expenditure, and household income;
